finding.title: OS Command Injection in SVGWriter::writeMarker
finding.assumptions: The SVG file is saved and later executed or rendered in an environment where the SVG content can trigger OS commands.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Verified that the sink is a file write: svgFile << "<marker id=\"" << markerId << "\" ...". The code does not invoke any shell, system, exec, or similar API that would execute markerId as a command. It merely emits SVG markup, so markerId cannot influence OS command execution. Thus the claim of OS Command Injection is unfounded.

finding.title: OS Command Injection in SVGWriter::writeLine
finding.assumptions: The SVG file is saved and later executed or rendered in an environment where the SVG content can trigger OS commands.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked the sink at lines 35-36: the untrusted source "markerStart" is directly concatenated into an SVG attribute value. No call to a system or shell command is made; the output is simply written to a file. SVG renderers treat the marker-start attribute as a URI reference to an SVG element ID, not as shell code. Even if the attacker supplies a value like "markerStart; touch /tmp/exploit", the resulting file contains the literal text "marker-start=\"url(#markerStart; touch /tmp/exploit)\"" which is not interpreted as an OS command by browsers or standard SVG viewers. Therefore no command execution can occur from this sink under normal use. No other checks or sanitization are present, but the absence of a command interpreter renders the reported CWE‑78 case invalid.
